subsection: 8. Demographic and social change: the status of women and social change, 1949–1989

notes.b: To follow how the status of women and Irish society changed between 1949 and 1989, you need to know how conservative the starting point was. Law, work and family life were all shaped by religion and by a stagnant economy.
points: Ireland in 1949 was a conservative, Catholic and mainly rural society, and the Catholic Church shaped the law and public attitudes on sex, marriage and the family.
The 1937 Constitution gave the family and the home a central place for women, so the law tended to treat a woman's main role as that of wife and mother.

The stagnant economy of the 1950s drove mass emigration. The turn to economic expansion from 1958, and Ireland's entry to the EEC (the European Economic Community, forerunner of the European Union) in 1973, then changed both the economy and the pressure for reform.

Contraception was banned: a law of 1935 forbade its sale and import, and the Church opposed artificial contraception, so the ban had strong moral backing, a position Pope Paul VI reaffirmed in his encyclical (a formal papal letter) of 1968.

Three key concepts run through the topic. Discrimination is unequal treatment on grounds such as sex or marital status. Liberalisation is the relaxing of legal or social restrictions, for example on contraception, censorship or homosexuality.
Equality of opportunity means the same access to education, jobs and promotion regardless of sex.
notes.tip: Define discrimination, liberalisation and equality of opportunity as they apply to Ireland in this period, not in general terms.

notes.b: For about a century Ireland's population had been falling or static. From the 1960s it began to grow, and the census figures are useful evidence of how the economy and emigration changed.
points: The census recorded 2,960,593 people in 1951 and 2,818,341 in 1961, a fall of about 140,000, and the cause was emigration, because many more people left than were born to replace them.
The population rose to about 2.88 million in 1966 and about 2.98 million in 1971, as net emigration (people leaving minus people arriving) fell and the birth rate remained high.
It then grew rapidly, to about 3.44 million in 1981 and about 3.54 million in 1986, the highest figure for about a century.
Births peaked at about 74,000 in 1980, and the population was young, with a large proportion under 25, which kept the birth rate high.
Growth slowed after 1986 because heavy emigration returned, and the 1991 census recorded a small fall to about 3.53 million.
notes.tip: For broad questions on social and economic change, use population figures as evidence and name the cause each time: the 1950s fall, the 1960s and 1970s growth, and the 1980s slowdown.

notes.b: Emigration is the key to the population story, because the economy decided whether young people stayed or left. It moved through four phases, each with a different cause.
points: 1950s: net emigration was about 400,000, and most emigrants were young people going to Britain for work, because the stagnant economy offered them few jobs at home.
1960s: economic expansion cut net emigration sharply, to about 80,000 for 1961 to 1966, because more jobs were available in Ireland.

1970s: the flow reversed and there was net inward migration of about 100,000 over the decade. Many of the arrivals were Irish emigrants returning home as Britain suffered recession and Ireland joined the EEC in 1973.
1980s: emigration returned, with around 200,000 net emigrants over the decade, as unemployment rose above 15 per cent in the mid-1980s.
The 1980s emigrants were often well educated, and they went to Britain, the United States, Australia and continental Europe, so Ireland lost skilled people as well as labour.
Emigration was a continuing feature of Irish society, and it shaped family life, because families were split across countries. It also caused rural depopulation and affected attitudes to politics.
notes.tip: Say what caused each change in emigration (economy, EEC entry, British recession, unemployment) rather than just listing the numbers.

notes.b: As people left farms and small villages for towns, the shape of Irish society changed. Marriage and family patterns changed with it.
points: The urban population passed half the total around 1971 (about 52 per cent), and more than a quarter of the people lived in the Dublin area by 1981.
New suburbs and towns such as Tallaght, Clondalkin and Blanchardstown absorbed people moving from the countryside, while small farms and rural villages lost population.
Marriage rates rose in the 1960s and 1970s, and people married at a younger age than in the 1950s, when late marriage and non-marriage were common.
Large families were the norm in the 1960s, but the fertility rate (the average number of children per woman) fell steadily afterwards, to close to replacement level by the late 1980s.
Falling family size was linked to more use of contraception, which was illegal to sell until the late 1970s, and to women's rising education and employment.

notes.h: The marriage bar and the Commission on the Status of Women
notes.b: Before the 1970s, the law and employers openly treated married women as less entitled to work. The Commission on the Status of Women turned complaints about this into a programme for reform.
points: The marriage bar was the rule requiring women in the civil service and other public posts to resign when they married, so a woman had to choose between marriage and a career.
The bar was removed for primary teachers in 1958 and for the civil service in 1973. Banks and other employers kept their own bars on married women.
Women were also paid less than men for similar work, which was a form of discrimination on grounds of sex.
The Commission on the Status of Women was set up by the Lynch government in 1970, after pressure from women's organisations, and it was chaired by Thekla Beere.
Its interim report in 1971 recommended equal pay, and its final report in December 1972 made 49 recommendations on equal pay, employment, education, family law and social welfare.
The report provided a programme for reform, so campaigners could point to official backing, and many of its recommendations were implemented during the 1970s and 1980s.
notes.tip: For short questions on the marriage bar, say what it was and when it was removed (1958 for primary teachers, 1973 for the civil service). For the Commission, give the 1972 report, its 49 recommendations and its influence.

notes.h: The women's movement and the contraceptive train
notes.b: From 1970 a new generation of women campaigned in public rather than quietly lobbying. Their most famous action put contraception on the national agenda.
points: The Irish Women's Liberation Movement was formed in 1970 by journalists and activists including Mary Kenny, Nell McCafferty, June Levine and Nuala Fennell.
Its manifesto Chains or Change (1971) demanded equal pay, equal education, contraception and legal changes for unmarried mothers and deserted wives.

On 22 May 1971 dozens of members travelled by train from Dublin to Belfast, bought contraceptives that were illegal to import into the Republic and returned openly to Connolly Station in Dublin, challenging customs officers to stop them.
The action attracted large media coverage, which made contraception a public issue. It was a protest, not a court case, and it did not change the law itself.
Later groups provided services that the state did not: Women's Aid, founded in 1974 to help victims of domestic violence, and the Well Woman Centre, opened in 1977.
Women's organisations also used the trade unions and the Council for the Status of Women to lobby ministers.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the contraceptive train (a 1971 protest) with McGee (a 1973 court case).

notes.h: Contraception: McGee, the 1974 bill and the 1979 Act
notes.b: The law on contraception was the most controversial issue in the status of women in the 1970s. It was legalised in stages, not by one event: a court ruling in 1973, an Act in 1979 and an amendment in 1985.
points: Mary McGee, a mother of four who was medically advised against another pregnancy, took a case against the State after customs seized contraceptive jelly sent to her from abroad.

In McGee v Attorney General, decided in December 1973, the Supreme Court found by four to one that the ban on importing contraceptives for her was unconstitutional, because it infringed the right to marital privacy.
McGee was about importing contraceptives for a married woman, so it did not legalise sale, which stayed restricted.
In 1974 the Fine Gael-Labour government introduced a bill to regulate contraceptives, but it was defeated when Taoiseach Liam Cosgrave voted against his own government's bill.

The Health (Family Planning) Act 1979, brought in by Charles Haughey as Minister for Health, allowed contraceptives to be sold on prescription to people with a bona fide (genuine) need for family planning. Haughey called it "an Irish solution to an Irish problem".
The Act was in operation in 1980, and a 1985 amendment allowed sale to people over 18 without prescription.
The Catholic Church officially opposed artificial contraception, a position reaffirmed by Pope Paul VI in 1968, but surveys suggested that many Irish married Catholics ignored the rule.
notes.tip: Give the sequence in order: McGee (1973), failed bill (1974), Health (Family Planning) Act (1979) with Haughey's phrase, then 1985, plus the Church's stance. Do not say one event legalised contraception, and do not treat the Church as the only obstacle.

notes.b: Campaigning, the Commission's report and EEC membership together pushed the state to make sex discrimination unlawful. Each Act tackled a different area of women's lives.
points: The Anti-Discrimination (Pay) Act 1974 required equal pay for men and women doing the same or similar work, taking effect from the end of 1975, in line with EEC requirements.
The Employment Equality Act 1977 made it unlawful to discriminate on grounds of sex or marital status in recruitment, training and promotion.

The Employment Equality Agency was set up under the 1977 Act to promote equality, investigate, research and advise the government. It did not decide individual complaints itself, and its powers were limited.
The Juries Act 1976 ended the exclusion of women from jury service, so women could now take part in trials as jurors.
The Family Home Protection Act 1976 stopped a husband selling the family home without his wife's consent, which protected wives who owned no property in their own name.
The Maternity Protection of Employees Act 1981 gave women the right to maternity leave and to return to their jobs, so having a baby no longer meant losing a post.
Social welfare was reformed in the 1980s to give married women equal treatment, under pressure from EEC law.
notes.tip: Do not list Acts without dates. For the 1974 Act give its name, year and one effect (equal pay for the same or similar work from the end of 1975). Equal pay did not happen in 1973: that is the year the civil service marriage bar ended.

notes.h: Women in politics and public life
notes.b: Legal equality did not quickly produce equal representation. Women stayed a small minority in politics, though a few broke through to ministerial office, and more women went out to work.
points: Women remained a small minority in the Dáil (the lower house of parliament): six sat after the 1977 election, and the number reached 14 by 1987.
Eileen Desmond of Labour, for example, became Minister for Health and Social Welfare in 1981, the first woman in a cabinet since Constance Markievicz.
Gemma Hussey of Fine Gael was Minister for Education from 1982 to 1987, and Nuala Fennell was a Minister of State for women's affairs from 1982.
More women entered the workforce, particularly married women, whose participation rate rose from about 5 per cent in 1961 to about 17 per cent in 1981.
Mary Robinson, a senator from 1969, was the most prominent woman in public life outside government, because she pressed reform from the Seanad and the courts.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Eileen Desmond (Labour, Health and Social Welfare 1981) with Barry Desmond, or Mary Robinson the senator and lawyer with Mary Robinson the President of 1990.

notes.b: Meehan was a trade unionist and campaigner who became the first head of the Employment Equality Agency. Her work was to make the new laws operate in practice.
points: Sylvia Meehan was born in Dublin in 1929, worked as a teacher, and was vice-president of the Association of Secondary Teachers, Ireland and chairperson of the women's committee of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions.
She was appointed in 1977 as the first chairperson of the new Employment Equality Agency, a post she held until 1992.

She was a participant in the enforcement of the equal pay and equal treatment laws, leading the agency as they were implemented and supervising research, investigations and advice on discrimination at work.
The agency's research into the position of girls and women in education, pay, maternity leave and childcare helped to shape later legislation.
Contemporaries regarded her as an effective and determined advocate, though employers and some politicians resisted the agency's findings.
Historians see her as a key figure in turning the 1970s equality laws into practice, though they stress that the agency's powers were limited.
notes.tip: Short questions reward who she was, a dated fact (first chair of the Employment Equality Agency, 1977 to 1992) and one achievement. For a contrast with Robinson, say Meehan worked through enforcement and Robinson through law and politics.

notes.b: Robinson was a lawyer and senator who used the courts and the Oireachtas (the Irish parliament) to challenge discriminatory law. Here her career is taken only to 1989.
points: Mary Robinson was born in Ballina, Co. Mayo, in 1944, graduated from Trinity College Dublin, was called to the bar in 1967, studied at Harvard and became Reid Professor of Law at Trinity at the age of 25.

She was elected to the Seanad (the upper house) for the University of Dublin in 1969 and served until 1989, as an independent. She campaigned there for women to serve on juries, a change enacted in the Juries Act 1976.
In the early 1970s she introduced private members' bills (bills brought by an individual member, not the government) to liberalise the law on contraception, which the Seanad refused to debate.
She later sought reform of the law on homosexuality. Neither the contraception bills nor this reform became law at the time.

As a barrister she took cases on behalf of individuals against the State, including a tax case brought by a married couple, which the Supreme Court decided in their favour in 1980, and the Airey case on legal aid, heard by the European Court in 1979.

She also took the case of the campaigner David Norris against the law criminalising homosexual acts. The Supreme Court upheld the law in 1983, the European Court of Human Rights found against Ireland in 1988, and the law changed in 1993.
She joined the Labour Party in 1976 and left it in 1985 in protest at the Anglo-Irish Agreement, and she was a Dublin city councillor from 1979 to 1983.
Contemporaries saw her as a liberal reformer and an able lawyer, attacked by conservatives and the church for her views but respected for her persistence.
Historians credit her with creating a legal and political basis for reform that prepared the way for the 1990s and her election as President in 1990.
notes.tip: Short parts reward a dated fact (senator 1969 to 1989) and one named achievement such as the bills or a case. Keep her to 1989: her presidency in 1990 is outside the period.

notes.h: Assessment: the extent of social change
notes.b: Examiners reward a judgement that change was real but uneven. Pair what was achieved with what was not, and show how contemporaries and historians differed.
points: Achievements: the marriage bar ended, equal pay and employment equality were legislated, contraception became legally available and women gained new organisations, rights and visibility.
Limits: women remained scarce in politics and senior jobs, pay gaps persisted, divorce and abortion remained prohibited and the church kept its influence.
Contemporary view: conservatives argued that the reforms threatened the family and Catholic values, whereas reformers saw the changes as too little and too slow.

Later view: historians see the period as the beginning of social liberalisation, driven by economic change, EEC law and campaigning, but argue that change was uneven and that Ireland remained more conservative than many European states in the 1980s.
notes.tip: Pair each achievement with a limit, add the views of conservatives, reformers and later historians, and name the pressures behind change (campaigners, the Commission, EEC membership).

The journey of 22 May 1971 in which women travelled to Belfast and brought contraceptives back to Dublin.
The 1973 Supreme Court case that recognised married couples' right to privacy and struck down the ban on importing contraceptives.
